doc.title: Bill Goodwin interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 28, 2025

title: Teaching and standing on the shoulders of earlier drummers
summary: Students who don't know the older masters, and Max Roach's remark about those who came before.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Well your students probably would do the same thing with you.

Most of them are too young to even know my oeuvre so to speak, or you know they knew about me and I was on the faculty of a jazz school so I was certainly well known but I wasn’t like, you know Jack DeJohnette or, you know, Tony Williams ‘cause they were all — I think that, I remember first teaching in the College of William Paterson and I asked somebody who their favorite older drummer was and they said Tony Williams. I said, “Tony Williams, that young guy?” He’s like four years younger than me.” I said, “He’s not an old master yet.” You know these are people that think that jazz started with John Coltrane.

[Inaudible] The things that led up to that — as Max Roach pointed out years ago when he was being complimented for his innovations on the drums, he said, “I’m just standing on the shoulders of those who came before.” And I firmly believe that. And I’ve tried to pass that on and hopefully they get it. These guys have like so much ability on the drums at their age and they’re like teenagers, like I was. They’re in school but they can really play the drums, you know, whereas I had to learn to play the drums when I was already a professional musician.
